citations.claim: Krivitsky, Larman and Flemm's *Org Topologies* primer describes this setup.
It aims at "keeping 100% of them 100% busy", and when one part is tuned on its own, "flow can get worse!"
The Scrum Guide says: "Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making."
Jones (*Evidence-based Software Engineering*) cites Goodhart's law: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes."
The Department of Energy's human-performance handbook treats human error as "the effect or symptom of deeper trouble in the system."

The Columbia accident board warned that fixing the part and replacing or retraining the individual leads to "a misguided and potentially disastrous belief that the underlying problem has been solved."
The US Forest Service's learning-review guide calls punishing people after an incident "the surest way to kill a learning culture."
Sidney Dekker, quoted in that guide, says people who are blamed "will tell fewer accounts."
Jones notes that people keep using software with faults if it gives them enough benefit.
The DOE handbook says an organisation "is perfectly tuned to get the performance it receives from the workforce."
"Faster, better, cheaper" was NASA's slogan in the 1990s.
The Columbia board traces how budget and schedule pressure from that era left the shuttle programme "operating too close to too many margins."
Systems thinkers call this "shifting the burden".
The quick fix is "easier and faster than creating an upstream solution" but "may actually impede our ability to invest time and energy to the fundamental solution."
The NHS Just Culture guide gives a simple test: would comparable colleagues have merged the same change under the same conditions? If so, "Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate".
The DOE handbook says: "A just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture."
The *Org Topologies* authors add that people "have to own – not rent – their change".
The *Open Kanban* guide's advice is to reduce the size of the batches we work on, and it warns: "An exhausted developer, manager or team are the perfect recipe for disaster."
The *Org Topologies* authors put it this way: "more output does not mean more outcomes."
Even the most AI-positive source here says to put AI money where the bottleneck is, and expects humans to spend more of their time monitoring the AI.
The Open Practice Library's guide to OKRs says stretch goals motivate people, citing a vendor figure of "3X increase in productivity in 12 months."
Jones says targets used to control people get gamed.
He also says software engineering has so little hard evidence that folklore has filled the gap, including the 28-to-1 developer productivity claim.
Part of this disagreement goes away on a close reading: the OKR version assumes the team sets its own goals and aims at outcomes.
*Org Topologies* is bullish.
It says expertise is no longer scarce and suggests you "Spin up another 10,000 agents."
Jones would ask to see the data, and none of the sources I'm using contain measured evidence on AI coding tools.
The DOE handbook keeps root-cause analysis, but asks what could have prevented the event rather than who caused it.
The Forest Service guide avoids saying what caused an event at all, and warns that formal recommendations can add complexity and increase risk.
The Columbia board named causes at two levels and made structural recommendations.
The NHS guide keeps a route to performance management for cases that fail its tests.
The Columbia board leaves personal accountability to a separate process.
The Forest Service guide keeps a strict wall between the learning review and any disciplinary action.
*Open Kanban* defines value as working, good-quality code.
Jones says customers put up with faults when the benefit is worth it.
*Org Topologies* says how you structure the organisation largely decides performance.
*Open Kanban* says to start where you are without changing roles or titles.
The Columbia board wrote: "Leaders create culture. It is their responsibility to change it."

ideas.idea: Developers on two or three squads at once pay a switching cost; the fewer things in progress, the faster each finishes
'Nobody idle' optimises utilisation, not flow; pull work from a limited queue instead of pushing to keep people busy
Overflowing sprints: plan to a forecast the team owns, not a target set from above; the Sprint Goal and commitment belong to the Developers
Difficult goals raise effort, but only with commitment and ability; a target with a bonus attached invites gaming the measure
Output isn't outcome: more features shipped doesn't mean the problem customers care about gets solved; feature bloat
A shared Definition of Done is the quality bar; work that doesn't meet it isn't released, which is where the marketing-engineering argument gets settled
Naming and punishing the developer who merged the release: a just-culture test asks whether a peer would have done the same, and treats the system that let it through as the finding
Blame drives reporting underground; the next near-miss won't be surfaced
Buying tools to 'do both' is a fix that fails or shifts the burden: it eases the symptom and leaves the overload in place
The first change is one constraint, not a programme: cut work in progress (or stop the stretch target), then look again
A disagreement among the sources: goal theory says difficult goals improve performance; the flow and respect-for-people sources say overload and unsustainable pace destroy it

note: Strong: every quotation checked verbatim (the four MISSING rows in the locations list are false hits on the answer's own scare-quoted phrases, not quotations). The two partials are overreach: Org Topologies describes the Resource topology, not multi-squad splitting as such, and 'Jones would ask' is speculation. No Definition of Done; the stretch-target disagreement is OKR-vs-Goodhart rather than goal theory vs overload; the first-change rationale is credited to just-culture sources, not to a constraint source.
